title: Devlens Research Summary: Rohingya camps grow less safe as aid shrinks, UNHCR's Q3 protection report finds
excerpt: UNHCR's July-September report records more abductions, trafficking and refoulement, a halt to new-arrival registration, and a 30-40% cut in community protection work.
content:
The protection situation in the 33 Rohingya camps in Cox's Bazar and on Bhasan Char got worse between July and September 2026, according to UNHCR's latest Quarterly Protection and Solutions Report, published on ReliefWeb on Wednesday (25 November). Serious security incidents rose, trafficking victims increased by a quarter, and registration of new arrivals was suspended, while funding cuts forced protection partners to scale back services. This summary sets out the main findings and what they mean for agencies working in the response.

The source

The report is UNHCR Bangladesh's quarterly update for Q3 2026 (July to September). It draws on UNHCR's own case data, the joint Government of Bangladesh–UNHCR population database and the Protection Sector's Q3 Joint Protection Monitoring Report, which combines monitoring by seven partners. It is 11 pages long. Devlens read the full report. Some figures are UNHCR's alone and others are sector-wide, and the report says several activity figures may count the same person more than once.

Where things stand

As of 30 September, the joint database counted 1,206,528 Rohingya refugees, of whom 78% are women and children and 12% have specific needs. Some 155,560 people have arrived since January 2025. A presence check on Bhasan Char in September confirmed 26,775 refugees on the island, 8% fewer than in December 2025, although 94% of them said they intended to stay, up from 91%.

Finding 1: the camps are less safe

The Protection Sector recorded 655 serious security incidents across all camps and Bhasan Char in Q3, a 39% rise on Q2, led by abductions and kidnapping for ransom. Through its own channels UNHCR counted 181 serious incidents, up 8% from 168. Abductions and kidnappings rose from 78 to 84, serious assaults from 66 to 70, and extortion nearly doubled from six to 11. Killings stayed at nine. UNHCR reported only two cases of forced recruitment, but warned this may mean recruitment is now happening out of sight; 23 recruitment-related meetings linked to the Myanmar conflict were reported.

Law enforcement rescued 13 abducted refugees in the quarter, compared with five in Q2, and 19 refugees were arrested in kidnapping and ransom investigations. UNHCR notes that the number of host community members arrested is not known.

Finding 2: borders are tighter and registration has stopped

Refoulement made up 31% of incidents in 2026, up from 14% in 2025, and for the first time affected people holding refugee cards. UNHCR recorded 360 refoulement incidents in Q3 during 23 border monitoring missions. On 15 September, the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC) suspended registration of new arrivals. According to UNHCR, new arrival families now have no access to food or assistance. No date has been set to resume enrolment. UNHCR says it is proposing a revised process with a bigger role for the RRRC's office and Camps-in-Charge.

Finding 3: trafficking and dangerous journeys are rising

UNHCR identified 162 trafficking victims in Q3, 25% more than in Q2. Domestic trafficking linked to economic hardship made up 75% of cases, up from 61%. Most victims (78%) were male, but among female victims promises of marriage were used in 56% of cases, up from 42%. Boat departures from Bangladesh more than doubled in the first nine months of 2026 compared with 2025: UNHCR confirmed 11 departures, 2,141 arrivals by sea, mainly in Malaysia, and 280 people dead or missing. In September a boat with 16 people, eight Rohingya and eight Bangladeshis, sank near Teknaf, killing two.

Finding 4: funding cuts are cutting protection

The sector avoided pipeline breaks, but reduced funding for the 2026 Joint Response Plan meant community-based protection activities fell by 30–40% by 30 September, affecting some 150,000 to 200,000 refugees. Only 21% of people with specific protection needs (30,322) received targeted support. UNHCR estimates that 150,000 children and adolescents remain at risk of abuse, exploitation and neglect, and more than 500,000 women and girls at risk of gender-based violence. To save money, UNHCR says it moved awareness work to digital and refugee-led channels, replaced fixed information centres with mobile teams and merged services into 280 multipurpose centres.

Finding 5: more violence at home, and more cases reported

Reported gender-based violence cases rose 15% from Q2, which UNHCR partly links to more outreach. Intimate partner violence was the most common context, linked to unemployment, drug use, polygamy, dowry disputes and online gambling, which refugees themselves raised. Online abuse also rose. Specialised child protection services reached 35% more children than in Q2, and 48% more unaccompanied and separated children. Complaints to UNHCR's feedback channels about protection rose 38%, to 26,244, and those about physical safety by 42%.

Finding 6: some gains in access to justice

The share of reported cases formally registered by authorities rose from 26% in Q2 to 51% in Q3, though nearly half still needed court action because of limited police follow-up. Refugees getting legal aid rose 45%; 13,627 got help on ongoing cases and legal work secured the release of 289 detainees, mostly held for moving outside the camps. In September the law ministry appointed a dedicated judge to the Human Trafficking Offence Prevention Tribunal in Cox's Bazar, and UNHCR and BLAST launched virtual court hearings so refugee and host community victims and witnesses can testify remotely. Refugees also reported delays, unofficial payments and informal settlement of serious crimes, and fear of retaliation kept many victims from going to court.

On solutions, UNHCR referred 741 refugees for resettlement, 98% of its annual quota, and 74 departed in the quarter, bringing 2026 departures to 244. Enrolment in UNHCR-supported education rose 17% to 10,026 students, 3,833 of them girls.

What it means for the development sector

  • Protection funding is the first to go. Cuts to prevention and community work are happening while risks rise, which is likely to raise the cost of response later.
  • The registration suspension leaves new arrivals without food or aid. Agencies may need to plan for an unregistered and more vulnerable group, and donors may need to press for a resumption date.
  • Trafficking is increasingly domestic and driven by hardship. Livelihood and cash programmes, and anti-trafficking work in host communities, are part of the protection answer.
  • The justice gains (a dedicated tribunal judge, virtual hearings, higher case registration) show what legal aid partners such as BLAST and BRAC can achieve, but witness protection is still missing.
  • The 2027 Joint Response Plan, which UNHCR says it is now preparing with the GBV and child protection sub-sectors, is the next chance to set protection priorities.

Limits of the evidence

Figures from UNHCR channels and from the wider Protection Sector are not the same and should not be compared directly. Rises in reported GBV and child protection cases may reflect better outreach as well as more incidents. Several activity numbers include repeat participants. The report covers the period before the International Court of Justice's 19 November judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar, which UNHCR flagged as a risk to plan for, and before the start of the sailing season in October.

The bottom line

By UNHCR's own account, Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh faced more abduction, trafficking and pushbacks in mid-2026, with fewer services to help them. The report shows the response trying to do more with less, but the 30–40% cut in community protection and the halt to new-arrival registration are gaps that efficiency measures do not close.
